4. The learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule submitted first, that as there was no laches on the part of the petitioner in prosecuting the appeal the order rejecting the memorandum should not have been passed. Secondly, that the order dated 10, 4.85 not being a penal order the order dated 27.4.85 was illegal. The learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, submitted that the impugned order does not suffer from any error of law and the prayer made in the application of the petitioner dated 27.4.1985 was rightly refused and the Memorandum was legally rejected as there was inexcusable laches on the part of the petitioner to prosecute the appeal and the memorandum was drawn up on a paper insufficiently stamped. He further drawing my attention to the petition submitted that as the decree was drawn on 8.12.84 and the memorandum of appeal was filed on 7.3.85 the petitioner had sufficient time to procure requisite amount of Court fee and upon the applications of the petitioner praying time to deposit the deficit court fee the court allowed him sufficient opportunity for depositing the same. In that view, of the matter, it can easily be said that the petitioner did not prosecute his case with due diligence and there was laches on his part to procure the deficit Court fee. The learned Advocate referring to the applications filed by the petitioner also submitted that in view of the prayer one after another seeking for adjournment for an indefinite period it cannot also be said that the petitioner was diligent in prosecuting the case. He further referring me to paragraph No. 13 of the present Revisional Application submitted that as there was delay of 200 days in filing this revisional application before this Court it further indicates that the petitioner was not at all diligent in prosecuting its case and the authority competent to accord sanction for money was not willing to prosecute the appeal. In the aforesaid circumstances, the petitioner was not entitled to get any relief from the Court. I have perused the application for time as well as the letters (annexed to this, petition) by which the petitioner prayed for payment of deficit Court fee from the authority namely the Director-General, Bangladesh and Deputy Commissioner, Patuakhali and also paragraph No. 13 of the petition. It is difficult for us to say what was reason for delay in moving the Court-from reading paragraph No. 13 of the Revisional Application. The learned Advocate for the petitioner so far as this delay is concerned submitted that due to the engagement of petitioner "in some other official works he was unable to have discussion with the Advocate at Barisal and Dhaka and as the petitioner being free from his official works went to his Advocate for filing this case the delay occupied in filing the application. The delay is not insignificant. It was for 200 days. The law enjoins that each day delay is to be explained which has not been done in this case. A general statement that the petitioner was engaged in some other official works is not a sufficient cause within the meaning of section 5 of the Limitation Act. Of course, the Court in dealing within an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act should be loath to adopt a doctrinaire approach to the question rather it should look on the plea of sufficient cause in a practical way to advance the cause of justice. In that event, the Court, of course, is to take into consideration the facts of each individual case. From the facts of this case as discussed above we do not find any reason to hold that the delay in this case was not the result of laches on the part of the petitioner. If priority is given to other official works in preference to filing duly a case against an order standing against him within the prescribed time it cannot be said that the petitioner was diligent in prosecuting the matter. More so when there were other persons competent to take step for filing the case in the office of the petitioner. Moreover, a litigant whether a Government agency or a private party stands on equal footing in the eye of law. In view of the aforesaid circumstances I do not find any force in the first contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the petitioner was diligent in prosecuting the case. 

 "149. Where the whole or any part of any fee prescribed for any document by the law for the time being in force relating to Court-fees has not been paid, the Court may in its discretion, at any stage, allow the person, by whom such fee is payable, to pay the whole or part, as the case may be, of such Court-fee; and upon such payment the document, in respect of which such fee is payable shall have the same force and effect as if such fee had been paid in the first instance". From a close examination of the aforesaid provisions of law it seems that there is no element of limitation and no such element can be imported into therein in order to deflect the discretion of the court into any guided channel in course of deciding application for allowing time to make up deficiency of Court fee. But this discretion is not an unfettered one. A court should not exercise in aid such discretion to a litigant who is negligent and not diligent in pursuing a matter in a court of law to mend his initial defect. He who wants to invoke the discretion of a Court must be prompt in his action so as to enable the court to give equitable relief. But in this case court after passing order on 16.4.85 did not deem it necessary to prolong the matter by giving further time and that is why Court ordered that the time given upto 27.4.85 was the last chance. The contention of the learned Advocate is that the order dated 16.4.1985 not being a penal order to the effect that in default to pay deficit court fee by 27.4.85 the Memorandum of Appeal would be rejected, the court committed an error in rejecting the memorandum of appeal on 27.4.85. The contention is unintelligible. Under section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure a court allowing any period for doing any act may in its discretion from time to time enlarge such period even after expiry of the period so granted. The language of section 149 does not contemplate such condition before making a final order or in other words a penal order, as contended by the learned Advocate, which is not a condition precedent to an order of rejection of memorandum of appeal by an Appellate Court. Neither the language of the Court Fees Act nor the language used in sections 148 and 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure enjoins a Court to pass such an order. The order dated 16.4.85 was not a final order and when on 27.4.85 the petitioner failed to deposit the deficit Court fee and filed again an application for time, the court, after hearing the parties rejected the same and the memorandum of appeal. In that view of the matter, I do not find any illegality in the said order nor can it be said that the petitioner was not given any opportunity in making up deficiency in the court fee and the order complained of was arbitrary and capricious.
